text: Chunce files the first recorded news report on a cave wall. A rival cave accuses him of bias.
Chunce witnesses the invention of the wheel and files it under "local interest."
Chunce interviews the Great Pyramid's project manager, who insists it will be finished "by the end of the month."
Chunce asks the builders of Stonehenge what it is for. Their answer remains under embargo.
Chunce reports that the large wooden horse outside Troy "poses no obvious threat."
Chunce enters the first Olympic footrace to get a better angle. He is disqualified for winning.
Chunce beats the messenger from Marathon to Athens by several hours, then holds the story out of professional courtesy.
Chunce spends an afternoon interviewing Socrates, who answers every question with another question. Filed as "no comment."
Chunce crosses the Alps with Hannibal and complains in print about the elephants' lack of professionalism.
Chunce attends the Senate on the Ides of March, having been told there would be a vote. Describes proceedings as "unusually decisive."
Chunce meets the Roman invasion on the beach and asks to see their press credentials.
Boudica burns down Chunce's Londinium office. He calls it "a dark day for press freedom."
Chunce reviews Hadrian's Wall: two stars. "Long, but lacks narrative."
Chunce publishes his obituary of the Western Roman Empire, which he had kept on file since 410.
Chunce reports on the raid at Lindisfarne. The Vikings describe their visit as "a cultural exchange."
Chunce is present when Alfred burns the cakes. Fish News runs it on the front page; the Danish invasion goes on page six.
Chunce refuses to be counted in the Domesday Book, citing the protection of sources.
Chunce attends the sealing of Magna Carta and asks whether it says anything about the press. It does not.
Chunce is the only man in Europe not to catch the plague. He credits "journalistic integrity."
Chunce stands between the lines at Agincourt to present both sides. Both sides respond.
Chunce is shown the printing press and warns it will be the end of proper cave-wall journalism.
Chunce reaches the Americas some weeks before Columbus. He is irritated to find people already there, none of whom have heard of him.
Chunce sits for a portrait with Leonardo and is painted over. Leonardo maintains the smile was always hers.
Chunce nails a correction to the Wittenberg church door beneath Luther's. Nobody reads it.
Chunce secures an exclusive with Henry VIII on the subject of marriage and asks that it be kept updated.
Chunce reports that the Spanish Armada has been "delayed by weather." In his view, it remains delayed.
Chunce reviews the premiere of Hamlet and criticises the lead for taking an age to reach a decision.
Galileo observes the moons of Jupiter. Chunce insists that one of them owes him money.
Asked whether he is a Roundhead or a Cavalier, Chunce replies that he is the news. Both sides imprison him.
Chunce drops an apple on Newton's head to move the story along. Newton publishes; Chunce keeps the apple.
Chunce covers the Acts of Union and asks both parties, twice, whether they are sure.
Britain skips eleven days to adopt the Gregorian calendar. Chunce uses them to catch up on his filing.
Chunce reports the Boston Tea Party as "a poorly catered event."
Chunce is found inside the Bastille when it is stormed. He declines to say how long he had been there.
Chunce signals Nelson's fleet: "Fish News expects every man to read it." The signal is not relayed.
Chunce attempts to amuse the young Queen Victoria. She is not.
Chunce exhibits himself at the Great Exhibition and is moved to the Curiosities section.
Chunce reads On the Origin of Species and informs Darwin that he was there for most of it.
Chunce reviews the new London Underground: "Dark, crowded, and running late. It will never catch on."
Chunce receives an early telephone call and lets it go to a messenger boy.
Chunce attends the first powered flight at Kitty Hawk and calls it "brief, but ambitious."
Chunce reaches the South Pole first and leaves a note that says "Already covered."
Chunce referees the Christmas truce football match. Both sides dispute the result to this day.
Chunce tells Howard Carter he saw the tomb when it was new, and that it was nicer then.
Chunce advises Fish News readers to "hold." Fish News declines to reprint the column.
Chunce appears in an early television broadcast and complains that nobody gave him his light.
Chunce reports from Roswell. The weather balloon declines to comment.
Chunce registers with the NHS on its first day. He remains on the waiting list.
The first sub-four-minute mile is run. Chunce, who paced the entire race, is not mentioned.
Chunce describes the Great Train Robbers as "well organised, if not especially punctual."
Asked whether the ball crossed the line, Chunce says he must consult his sources. He is still consulting.
Chunce is photographed on top of the Berlin Wall. He says he had been up there since 1961, waiting for the story to develop.
Chunce walks through the Channel Tunnel before it opens and reports that France is "much as I left it."
Chunce warns of the Millennium Bug. Nothing happens, and Chunce takes the credit.
Chunce reviews the Millennium Dome. He says he has seen better domes, and lists eleven.
Chunce files the end of the world on schedule and issues a correction the next morning.
Chunce files a report on the Fish News office's thousand-year lease renewal. Readers are asked not to question the lease.
Chunce files his final report from the heat death of the universe. His editor asks him to make it shorter.
